articles.title: Women's criminal records wiped for abortion offences
articles.summary: Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new atomatic pardons come into force in England and Wales.
articles.content:
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.

Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".

"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.

"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."

Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."

It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.

"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.

It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant legal and human rights advancement in England and Wales, where women previously criminalized for abortion offenses are now receiving automatic pardons and their criminal records wiped. This change addresses outdated and harmful laws, reduces trauma for affected women, and improves reproductive rights and justice on a broad societal scale.
articles.personality_title: England and Wales erase criminal records for abortion offenses
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In England and Wales, women who were arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions faced serious criminal charges under old laws. These laws often caused lasting harm to women who sought to end pregnancies.

**What happened** – New automatic pardons have been introduced, wiping the criminal records of women convicted or arrested for abortion offenses. This change follows cases like Nicola Packer’s, who was cleared after a long trial. Nicola took abortion pills prescribed by phone during Covid but was accused of ending a pregnancy later than allowed. She was found not guilty after jurors spent hours deciding the case.

**Impact** – The new pardons mean women will no longer carry the burden of a criminal record for abortion-related offenses. This helps reduce trauma and stigma. It also shows a shift away from outdated laws that treated women unfairly. Nicola’s story highlights how the old rules could harm women physically and emotionally, even when they followed medical advice.

**What’s next step** – With these pardons in place, women’s rights around pregnancy choices are better protected. The change may encourage more updates to laws that affect reproductive health, making healthcare safer and fairer.

**One-sentence takeaway** – England and Wales have taken an important step by clearing the records of women punished under old abortion laws, improving justice and support for reproductive choices.
articles.personality_title_fr: Angleterre et Pays de Galles effacent les casiers judiciaires liés à l'avortement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Angleterre et au Pays de Galles, les femmes arrêtées ou condamnées pour avortements illégaux faisaient face à de lourdes charges pénales en vertu de lois anciennes. Ces lois causaient souvent des souffrances durables aux femmes qui souhaitaient interrompre une grossesse.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – De nouvelles grâces automatiques ont été mises en place, effaçant les casiers judiciaires des femmes condamnées ou arrêtées pour des infractions liées à l'avortement. Ce changement fait suite à des cas comme celui de Nicola Packer, acquittée après un long procès. Nicola avait pris des pilules abortives prescrites par téléphone pendant le Covid, mais était accusée d'avoir mis fin à une grossesse au-delà du délai légal. Le jury l'a déclarée non coupable après plusieurs heures de délibération.

**Impact** – Ces nouvelles grâces signifient que les femmes ne porteront plus le poids d'un casier judiciaire pour des infractions liées à l'avortement. Cela aide à réduire les traumatismes et la stigmatisation. Cela montre aussi un recul des lois dépassées qui traitaient les femmes injustement. L’histoire de Nicola montre comment les anciennes règles pouvaient nuire aux femmes, même quand elles suivaient les conseils médicaux.

**Prochaine étape** – Avec ces grâces, les droits des femmes sur leurs choix de grossesse sont mieux protégés. Ce changement pourrait encourager d’autres mises à jour des lois touchant la santé reproductive, rendant les soins plus sûrs et plus justes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’Angleterre et le Pays de Galles ont franchi une étape importante en effaçant les casiers judiciaires des femmes punies sous d’anciennes lois sur l’avortement, améliorant la justice et le soutien aux choix reproductifs.
articles.personality_title_es: Inglaterra y Gales borran antecedentes penales por delitos de aborto
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Inglaterra y Gales, las mujeres arrestadas o condenadas por abortos ilegales enfrentaban cargos penales graves bajo leyes antiguas. Estas leyes a menudo causaban daño duradero a las mujeres que querían interrumpir un embarazo.

**Qué pasó** – Se han introducido indultos automáticos que borran los antecedentes penales de mujeres condenadas o arrestadas por delitos relacionados con el aborto. Este cambio sigue casos como el de Nicola Packer, quien fue absuelta tras un largo juicio. Nicola tomó pastillas abortivas prescritas por teléfono durante la Covid, pero fue acusada de interrumpir un embarazo después del tiempo permitido. El jurado la declaró inocente después de varias horas de deliberación.

**Impacto** – Los nuevos indultos significan que las mujeres ya no cargarán con antecedentes penales por delitos relacionados con el aborto. Esto ayuda a reducir el trauma y el estigma. También muestra un alejamiento de leyes desactualizadas que trataban injustamente a las mujeres. La historia de Nicola destaca cómo las viejas reglas podían dañar a las mujeres física y emocionalmente, incluso cuando seguían consejos médicos.

**Próximo paso** – Con estos indultos, los derechos de las mujeres sobre sus decisiones de embarazo están mejor protegidos. El cambio podría impulsar más actualizaciones en leyes que afectan la salud reproductiva, haciendo la atención médica más segura y justa.

**Resumen en una frase** – Inglaterra y Gales han dado un paso importante al borrar los antecedentes penales de mujeres castigadas bajo antiguas leyes de aborto, mejorando la justicia y el apoyo a las decisiones reproductivas.

articles.title: Empowering faith and Indigenous leaders to combat hate
articles.summary: Religious, traditional and Indigenous leaders need to be empowered to act as full partners in preventing conflict, not just praised for their role, speakers said Sunday at the opening of the Muscat Plan of Action Forum in Oman.
articles.content:
Key points

The Muscat Plan of Action Forum was timed with the International Day for Tolerance , marked annually on 16 November

Young people from more than 20 countries are taking part in a mediation training programme

Workshops aim to produce a global framework for putting the plan into practice

UN officials, community leaders, Indigenous representatives and young people from around the world have gathered to find practical local, regional and international steps for carrying out the Muscat Plan of Action, launched last June by Oman, the United Nations and international partners.

The forum’s theme, From international commitment to local impact: Prevention and peacebuilding, covers three areas: leadership and prevention, dialogue and cohesion and partnerships and implementation.

Read the full Muscat Plan of Action here.

‘Trust of communities’

Peace does not come simply from ending conflicts or signing agreements, Mohamed bin Said bin Khalfan Al-Maamari, Oman’s Minister of Endowments and Religious Affairs, told leaders.

Instead, it rests on trust, shared values and a community’s ability to manage its differences without hostility, Mr. Al-Mamari said.

“What we need today is for the legitimacy of institutions to be integrated with the trust of communities and for specialised knowledge to meet inherited wisdom,” he said.

Such leaders know their communities and have their trust, he continued, so they can reach people that official channels often cannot.

Prevention before violence

Chaloka Beyani, the UN Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide, emphasised that traditional and Indigenous leaders must be involved in countering hate speech and incitement and in preventing mass atrocities.

In the same vein, former Finnish President Tarja Halonen warned that intolerance and hate speech deepen divisions and, in the worst cases, lead to atrocities. Prevention, she said, must begin long before conflict breaks out.

“Hate speech can make discrimination seem more acceptable and gradually turn neighbours into enemies,” Ms. Halonen said, urging leaders to defend people targeted for their identity, beliefs or ethnic background.

She also praised the plan’s focus on women and youth and called for close cooperation among governments, communities, international institutions, faith leaders and civil society.

‘Harming others is harming oneself’

Sonia Astuhuaman Pardave leads Indigenous women from the Quechua people of the Wanka Nation and serves as women’s counsellor at the organisation CAOI.

She said Indigenous philosophy rests on mutual giving, gratitude and respect for all life.

“Harming others is harming oneself,” she said, adding that Indigenous peoples defend their rights through community organising, spirituality and legal action, not violence.

UN News/Abdelmonem Makki

Youth as partners

Alongside the forum, young people from more than 20 countries are taking part in Oman’s Harmonious Connections, a training course in religion and mediation.

Mohamed Elsanousi, Executive Director of the Network for Religious and Traditional Peacemakers, said many of the participants already work as peacebuilders in their own communities.

Florencio, from Colombia, has spent nearly 10 years helping underrepresented groups take part in international processes. He said young people are among those hit hardest by conflict but are also able to find solutions.

Kelly Ketchedjian, a Lebanese student of international relations, said the course covered gender-based violence and how to analyse conflicts.

“We are not just children of Lebanon, we are children of the world,” she said.

From dialogue to action

The forum’s workshops aim to produce a global implementation framework, along with practical steps at the regional, national and local levels.

The plan treats local communities as key partners in prevention.

It also calls for responses suited to each community’s circumstances, with dialogue, mediation and confidence-building used to keep tensions from turning into conflict.

Find out more about UN efforts to combat hate speech here.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant international initiative empowering faith, traditional, and Indigenous leaders to prevent conflict and hate speech, promoting peacebuilding and social cohesion. articles.title: Nadia Murad: ‘Day by day, I took my story back’
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Nadia Murad has spent years telling the world about the atrocities committed against her and the Yazidi community by militants from the terrorist group, ISIL.
articles.content:
But now, she wants to tell her story beyond survival, having broken the stigma surrounding conflict-related sexual violence and moved on from her pioneering role as the first UN Goodwill Ambassador for the Dignity of Survivors of Human Trafficking, just over two years ago.

Over eight years of powerful advocacy working with the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) – she ensured that survivors are recognised not simply as victims, but as leaders with the power to shape change.

This week, Ms. Murad returned to UN Headquarters in New York, for a packed event at the UN Bookshop focused on her new memoir, I Choose My Beginning – a deeply personal account of rebuilding her life.

Turning the page

ISIL, also known by the Arabic moniker Daesh, conducted a genocidal campaign beginning in August 2014 against the Yazidis, whose historic homeland is the Sinjar region of northern Iraq.

Ms. Murad’s first book, The Last Girl: My Story of Captivity and My Fight Against the Islamic State, focused on that 2014 genocide where six of her brothers were murdered and she was taken into sexual slavery in Mosul – one of over 6,000 Yazidi women taken captive, according to UN figures. She escaped after three months, reaching a camp in Kurdistan and was then resettled in Germany.

With her new book, she said, she wanted to explore a different part of her journey – one centred on healing, relationships, love and the possibility of building a future.

“I was just another story – part of a global community of survivors of rape, men, women and children from all around the world” she said, recalling the early years of her advocacy.

She described how repeated public appearances and interviews left her feeling that she was disappearing into activism.

At certain point, Ms. Murad felt that she had lost herself – the girl who grew up on a farm, in a big family, was gone.

“I was disappearing, even physically, my hair was falling, I was losing weight, not sleeping, not eating” – but the fact that her niece and best friend was still in captivity kept her going, with the hope it would help rescue her.

“Day by day, I took it back piece by piece, I built it. - Nadia Murad

When her niece Kathrine was killed, she lost faith in humanity for the first time. “I couldn’t do it anymore.”

‘The world failed me’

Her family came together to remind her that she could feel safe again, get educated and pursue life beyond activism. “Finding love also changed me”, Ms. Murad explained.

In her book she writes that the first time she told her story, she felt it did not belong to her. “Day by day, I took it back piece by piece, I built it.”

“What they did to us was their legacy,” she said of ISIL’s three-year rule of terror, which “was the permanent mark that rape leaves on your body, on your mind.”

UN Publications/Steven Bornholtz

Survivors are blameless but you will always wrestle with your own memories: “I didn’t do anything wrong. The world failed me”, she added.

Push for justice

Nadia Murad came to the UN Security Council in 2015 to testify, and she recounted the atrocities committed against the Yazidi community and called for international action against human trafficking and sexual violence in conflict.

The UN system has sought to address sexual violence not only as a consequence of conflict, but as a crime that must be prevented and prosecuted.

For Ms. Murad, the response must go further: survivors must be seen not only through the violence they have endured, but as individuals with ideas – and the capacity to lead change.

Ms. Murad also called for survivors to be included in policy discussions as leaders and experts: “If we keep treating them as just victims and expect them to just never recover, we’re never going to prevent this from happening,” she told the audience.

A source of inspiration

Academy Award-winning actress and current UNODC Goodwill Ambassador to Combat Trafficking, Mira Sorvino, was at the bookshop too and praised Ms. Murad for challenging the tendency to see survivors only in relation to their trauma.

Ms. Sorvino, who also serves on the board of trustees of the UN Voluntary Trust Fund for Victims of Trafficking in Persons, said Ms. Murad had transformed unimaginable suffering and trauma into a source of strength and inspiration for others.

“She’s basically taking ownership of all the negativity of her life, and all the kind of public fascination that feeds on distress and feeds on trauma (…) and turned this on its head”.

“Her story is not the terrible things that were inflicted on her,” Ms. Sorvino said, reflecting on the message of the new book. Rather, it is about reclaiming life and rebuilding in the face of what happened.

“Unfortunately, Nadia can’t be the last girl – as conflicts and atrocities continue – but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth fighting for,” she added.

Ms. Sorvino shared her own experience as a survivor of sexual violence, saying that Ms. Murad’s courage had given her strength and underscored the importance of speaking out.

In her book, Ms. Murad writes: “Survivors, though, are changing. We are becoming bolder and more vocal, less likely to let the stigma of rape push us into some dark, silent hole.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: Nadia Murad shares new memoir to reclaim her story and inspire change
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Nadia Murad is a Nobel Peace Prize winner and a survivor of terrible violence committed by the terrorist group ISIL against the Yazidi community in northern Iraq. She has spent years speaking out about these crimes and fighting for justice.

**What happened** – Nadia recently returned to the United Nations in New York to talk about her new book, "I Choose My Beginning." This memoir focuses on her life after surviving captivity and violence, showing how she rebuilt herself through healing, love, and hope. She also spoke about moving beyond being seen only as a victim to becoming a leader.

**Impact** – Nadia’s story is important because it changes how people see survivors of violence. Instead of just victims, she shows they can be strong leaders who help make laws and policies to stop these crimes. Her work with the UN has helped survivors have a voice and be part of important decisions. This new book highlights the personal side of healing, encouraging others to find strength after trauma.

**What's next step** – Nadia and the UN want more survivors to be included in discussions about how to prevent and punish sexual violence and human trafficking. Her example may inspire more survivors to speak out and lead change worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Nadia Murad’s new memoir shows how survivors can reclaim their lives and become powerful voices for justice and healing.
articles.personality_title_fr: Nadia Murad publie un nouveau livre pour reprendre le contrôle de son histoire et inspirer le changement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Nadia Murad est lauréate du prix Nobel de la paix et survivante de violences terribles commises par le groupe terroriste ISIL contre la communauté yézidie dans le nord de l’Irak. Elle a passé des années à témoigner de ces crimes et à lutter pour la justice.

Ce mémoire parle de sa vie après avoir survécu à la captivité et à la violence, montrant comment elle s’est reconstruite grâce à la guérison, l’amour et l’espoir. Elle a aussi expliqué qu’elle voulait dépasser l’image de victime pour devenir une leader.

**Impact** – L’histoire de Nadia est importante parce qu’elle change la façon dont on voit les survivants de violences. Au lieu d’être seulement des victimes, elle montre qu’ils peuvent être des leaders forts qui aident à créer des lois pour arrêter ces crimes. Son travail avec l’ONU a permis aux survivants d’avoir une voix et de participer aux décisions importantes. Ce nouveau livre met en lumière la guérison personnelle et encourage d’autres personnes à trouver la force après un traumatisme.

**Prochaine étape** – Nadia et l’ONU veulent que davantage de survivants soient inclus dans les discussions pour prévenir et punir les violences sexuelles et la traite des êtres humains. Son exemple pourrait inspirer plus de survivants à s’exprimer et à mener le changement dans le monde.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Le nouveau mémoire de Nadia Murad montre comment les survivants peuvent reprendre leur vie en main et devenir des voix puissantes pour la justice et la guérison.
articles.personality_title_es: Nadia Murad comparte nuevo libro para recuperar su historia e inspirar cambio
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Nadia Murad es ganadora del Premio Nobel de la Paz y sobreviviente de violencia terrible cometida por el grupo terrorista ISIL contra la comunidad yazidí en el norte de Irak. Ha pasado años hablando sobre estos crímenes y luchando por la justicia.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, Nadia regresó a las Naciones Unidas en Nueva York para hablar sobre su nuevo libro, "Elijo mi comienzo". Este libro cuenta su vida después de sobrevivir el cautiverio y la violencia, mostrando cómo se reconstruyó a través de la sanación, el amor y la esperanza. También habló sobre dejar de ser vista solo como víctima para convertirse en líder.

**Impacto** – La historia de Nadia es importante porque cambia cómo se ven a los sobrevivientes de violencia. En lugar de solo víctimas, muestra que pueden ser líderes fuertes que ayudan a crear leyes para detener estos crímenes. Su trabajo con la ONU ha ayudado a que los sobrevivientes tengan voz y participen en decisiones importantes. Este nuevo libro destaca la parte personal de la sanación, animando a otros a encontrar fuerza después del trauma.

**Próximo paso** – Nadia y la ONU quieren que más sobrevivientes participen en discusiones sobre cómo prevenir y castigar la violencia sexual y la trata de personas. Su ejemplo puede inspirar a más sobrevivientes a hablar y liderar cambios en todo el mundo.

**Mensaje en una frase** – El nuevo libro de Nadia Murad muestra cómo los sobrevivientes pueden recuperar sus vidas y convertirse en voces poderosas por la justicia y la sanación.
